That indeed can be true. I learned a lot about Japan playing Shingen the Ruler or Nobunaga's Ambition. But in life opportunity cost plays a role. Time playing video games is time not reading a book or cultivating a meaningful relationship. I can learn more authentic history reading good, relevant books on the subject than I can playing some RPG. That's a fact and if one wants to learn deeply about philosophy or politics there is no substitute for reading.

Video games are useful for kids in that they improve hand-eye coordination and such but any lessons they teach are, again, inferior to sources like reading good books. Like me playing Nobunaga they serve as an introduction to serious history - and I have read some on Japanese history and culture.

So the takeaway is if a guy is still playing video games when he's old enough that he should be focusing on more meaningful pursuits it's a kind of extended adolescence.

While you say many true things here, I overall disagree to the extent that I think (and have occasionally see news items come along mentioning this) that video games are in fact (in moderation, of course) good for the elderly, in a similar way that crossword puzzles are. Of course, there are a lot of men in their prime who spend way too much of their resources (time, money) on gaming that they'd better invest in getting educated and/or raising a family. So, it is a problem. But in my perception not to the extent you seem to be seeing it.

Besides, as several posters already mentioned, gaming is just a form of escapism. It is less passive (though I admit possibly more absorbing, and hence more addictive) than binge-watching tv or movies.

I've in the past thought of taking up games again when I'm elderly as I did when I was a child. But those two periods in life are sort of similar in that the brain is not at an optimum level. The prime of life should be for higher pursuits as you've suggested.
